messages.text: Which tool would be the best to make something similar to vampire survivors, a.k.a like a 2d dungeon crawler with random items and spells?

ChatGPT said:

If you want “Vampire Survivors–style” (top-down 2D, tons of enemies, random item/spell builds, lots of simple projectiles, fast iteration), the “best tool” mostly depends on how fast you want to get playable vs how deep you want to go later.

Best overall pick (especially for solo / small teams)

Godot (4.x)

Why it fits this genre: insanely quick iteration for 2D, good scene system, great for “spawn a million things + UI + upgrades + loot tables,” easy to write systems for random items/spells.
Performance note: you can push a lot of entities, but for “thousands of enemies/projectiles” you’ll want pooling, lightweight collisions, and maybe custom batching—still very doable.
Best if you want industry-standard + lots of learning resources

Unity (2D)

Why it fits: endless tutorials/assets, proven for this exact type of game, strong tooling, easy to scale into more complex content pipelines.
Tradeoff: more “engine overhead” and project complexity; you’ll spend more time wrangling architecture and settings than in Godot.
Best if you want to code-first and keep it lightweight

LÖVE (Love2D) (Lua)

Why it fits: extremely fast to prototype, simple, minimal friction, great if you like building your own systems (waves, loot tables, spell modifiers).
Tradeoff: you build more stuff yourself (editor tooling, some conveniences).
Best if you want super-fast prototyping with an all-in-one editor

GameMaker

Why it fits: quick to make a playable 2D game, good workflow for sprites/rooms/UI, popular for arcade-y 2D.
Tradeoff: scaling to very “system-heavy” roguelite meta can be totally fine, but some people eventually wish they were in Godot/Unity for large architecture.
Best for web (playable in browser)

Phaser (JavaScript/TypeScript)

Why it fits: 2D action in the browser, easy to share instantly, nice if you want it on itch.io as HTML5.
Tradeoff: you’ll do more “engineering” yourself vs a full engine.
My practical recommendation
If you want to ship something like Vampire Survivors with minimal pain: Godot.
If you want the most tutorials + asset ecosystem and don’t mind more overhead: Unity.
If you want pure coding speed / minimalist vibe: LÖVE.

If you tell me:

your coding comfort level (beginner / comfy / strong),
target platform (PC only? mobile? web?),
…I’ll point to one choice and give you a “first 7 days build plan” (movement → spawners → upgrades → RNG items → meta progression).
Beginner I guess and pc, so maybe I could put it on steam. Also I would want it to have like "cutscenes" between parts

ChatGPT said:

Beginner + PC + “eventually Steam” + cutscenes between parts → I’d steer you to Godot.

Why Godot fits your exact combo
Beginner-friendly loop: you can get a playable prototype fast (movement → enemies → XP → upgrades) without fighting engine complexity.
2D-first workflow: scenes/nodes make “a thousand little game objects” easier to reason about.
Cutscenes are built-in-friendly: you can do them with:
AnimationPlayer (camera pans, fades, character poses, scripted beats)
Dialog / VN-style sequences (text boxes, portraits, choices)
Timeline-style plugins later if you want fancier sequencing (but you can start with zero plugins).
What “cutscenes” usually look like in this genre (and how you’d implement them)

You typically want short, cheap, stylish cutscenes:

Between stages: fade → 2–4 lines of dialogue → maybe a camera move → next run
Boss intro: lock player → pan camera → show boss name → “GO”
Meta progression story beats: after unlock X, play a small scene

In Godot, the clean beginner path is:

Make a Cutscene scene (UI + optional camera overlay)
Feed it a small script/data file (lines, portraits, triggers)
When the cutscene ends, emit a signal like cutscene_finished(next_stage_id)

This keeps cutscenes separate from combat code, which matters a lot once your project grows.

Steam angle

Both Godot and Unity can ship to Steam fine. Godot is totally viable for a first commercial PC game, especially a 2D one.

When I’d pick Unity instead

If you really want:

the biggest tutorial ecosystem for every single thing,
lots of premade assets/tools,
or you plan to hire/scale later and want the most common engine in job pools.

But for you, right now, Unity tends to feel like “learning the engine” before “making the game.”

A simple starter plan (so you don’t drown)

If you go Godot:

Player movement + aim
Enemy spawner + basic chase AI
Auto-attacks (projectiles / melee pulse)
XP gems + level-up screen
Random upgrade rolls (3 choices)
Cutscene system (simple dialogue + fade + trigger)
One full stage loop (win/lose → meta unlock)

If you want, I can give you a “minimum viable cutscene system” design (scene structure + signals + tiny data format) that won’t turn into spaghetti once you add more story beats.
Would it be possible to make it like there is 6 item slots, which upon dying would disappear as rogue like, but 3 spell card slots which would stay after death?

ChatGPT said:

Yeah—totally doable, and it’s a good roguelite structure because it creates two progression layers:

Run layer (roguelike): 6 item slots = temporary power, lost on death.
Meta layer (roguelite): 3 spell card slots = persistent build identity, kept after death.
How to model it cleanly (engine-agnostic, works great in Godot)

Think in terms of two inventories + two save scopes:

1) Run Inventory (temporary)
run_items[6]
Stored in a “RunState”
On death: wiped / regenerated next run

Examples: +damage items, drones, orbitals, on-hit effects, armor, crit, speed.

2) Meta Spell Deck (persistent)
persistent_spells[3]
Stored in a “Profile” / “SaveData”
On death: stays

Examples: your core spells that define how you play (fireball, chain lightning, curse aura), maybe upgradable permanently over time.

What happens on death (the exact behavior you want)

On player death:

Clear run_items (and any run-only upgrades)
Keep persistent_spells unchanged
Start a new run with the same 3 spells equipped

That’s the “feel” you’re describing.

Design details that make this feel right

Here are the big choices (you can pick any; they all work):

A) How spells interact with items

Best-feeling approach:

Spells are the base kit (always active / always available).
Items are modifiers that can upgrade spells or add new effects.

Example:

Persistent spell: “Magic Missile”
Run item: “Split Shot” → missiles split into 2
Run item: “Poison Ink” → missiles apply poison

So spells persist, but the run still feels fresh because items mutate them.

B) How you unlock/upgrade persistent spells

Good roguelite loop:

You start with 1–2 spells available.
You unlock more via meta currency.
You can upgrade spells between runs (rank 1 → rank 2).
Optionally: you can “prestige” a spell for a new modifier.
C) Preventing the “always same build” problem

Because spells persist, you’ll want variability. Common solutions:

Spell cards have downsides (tradeoffs).
Spell slots have synergies (set bonuses).
New runs offer random “spell augments” that are temporary.
Implementation structure (simple and beginner-friendly)

You’ll want 3 data buckets:

SaveData (persistent, written to disk)
equipped_spells[3]
unlocked spells
meta currency
RunState (temporary, reset each run)
items[6]
level, xp
temporary buffs/modifiers
PlayerCombat (runtime)
reads equipped_spells from SaveData
reads items from RunState
combines them to produce attacks

This separation keeps your game from becoming a spaghetti monster.

UI you’ll want
HUD: 6 item slots + 3 spell card slots
On death screen:
show items fading/shattering (lost)
show spells staying lit (kept)
This communicates the rule instantly without explaining it.

If you tell me how you imagine spells working (auto-cast like Vampire Survivors? cooldown abilities? mana?), I’ll propose a concrete system for:

what “spell cards” look like,
how they scale,
how items modify them,
and a simple saving/loading plan that’s safe and beginner-proof.

I thought for items that there would be set bonuses, for spells not so much. Also, that you would be able to choose from like "4 different races" and then there would be melee option, ranged option or "magic" option at the start

ChatGPT said:

Yep — that structure works, and it actually solves the “spells persist so runs feel samey” problem, because set-bonus items can be the main run-identity shifter.

Here’s a clean way to wire your idea together.

Core loop you’re describing
Pick Race (4 choices)
Pick Starting style: Melee / Ranged / Magic
Start run with your 3 persistent spell cards (your “signature kit”)
During the run you fill 6 item slots (temporary)
Items belong to sets, and sets grant bonuses at 2/3/4 pieces (etc.)
Die → items vanish, spells remain, race/style choice happens again next run (unless you want race persistent too)
1) Set bonuses for items: how to make it feel good

You want sets to be tempting but not mandatory. A good pattern:

Item sets (examples of thresholds)
2 pieces: small identity nudge
4 pieces: big gameplay change
6 pieces: “build-defining capstone” (rare but hype)

Example sets:

Bloodsteel (melee leaning)

2: +attack speed
4: melee hits cause bleed stacks
6: bleed pops explode in a cone

Galehunter (ranged leaning)

2: projectiles +pierce 1
4: every 5th shot fires a fan
6: crits summon homing shards

Starweave (magic leaning)

2: cooldown reduction
4: spells chain to extra targets
6: spells leave lingering zones
Important balancing trick

Sets should be cross-style compatible, not “this set only works for melee.”
Instead:

each set has a theme (bleed, chain, poison, frost, crit, summon, etc.)
melee/ranged/magic each has a different way to exploit that theme.

That gives you variety without hard-locking players.

2) Spells: persistent, but not “set bonus”

Totally fine. Spells can be your “loadout,” while items are the “run mutation.”

To keep spells interesting long-term, do one of these (pick 1):

Spell ranks (permanent upgrades: rank 1 → 2 → 3)
Spell modifiers (choose 1 of 2 variants permanently: “Fireball: bigger” vs “Fireball: faster”)
Spell mastery (use spell a lot → unlock tiny passive improvements)

No need for set bonuses here.

3) Race + Style pick at run start

This is strong because it gives players a quick identity choice before RNG takes over.

How to structure it cleanly
Race = passive identity
small baseline perks + maybe one unique mechanic
Style (melee/ranged/magic) = starting weapon + early rules
how you deal damage in minute 1
affects which item drops are more likely early (not exclusive)
Example design (concrete)

4 races (simple but distinct):

Human: versatile
+5% to all stats, reroll shop once per level-up
Elf: precision / mobility
+move speed, +crit chance, dash cooldown lower
Orc: brawler
+max HP, +lifesteal on close hits, armor scaling
Undead: risk/reward
heals less from normal sources, but gains power when low HP / on kill chains

3 styles (start kit):

Melee: short-range weapon, cleave arc, bonus armor early
Ranged: bow/gun, kiting bonuses, projectile speed/pierce early
Magic: basic spell wand, cooldown reduction early, mana/overheat system optional
The trick that makes this work with your persistent spell cards

Let style determine how your spells are triggered, not which spells you can have.

Example:

Melee style: spells trigger on hit / on kill / on combo meter
Ranged style: spells trigger on crit / on reload / on headshot (or “every N shots”)
Magic style: spells trigger on cooldown normally, or get boosted effects

So the same 3 persistent spells feel different depending on style. Huge replay value.

4) Drop system: how to support set-building

If sets matter, you need the game to help players complete them sometimes.

Good approach:

Items have rarity
Items have set tags
Each level-up offers:
1 item from a set you already have (soft “pity” system)
1 random item
1 “counter-pick” defensive item

This makes set-building feel intentional without being guaranteed.

Implementation note (so it stays beginner-friendly)

You’ll want your items and sets as data, not hardcoded logic.

Item definition: name, icon, stats, set_id
Set definition: thresholds → effects
Every time items change, recalc:
count pieces per set
apply thresholds

That’s very doable in Godot/Unity without advanced math.

If you want, I can propose:

4 race passives (balanced, not bloated)
3 styles with starting weapons + a simple “spell trigger” rule per style
6–8 item sets with thresholds and effects
…all in one cohesive starter roster so you can prototype fast.

But the biggest thing would be super randomizer, okay, now it's in extremes but the item stats for the character or creatures could go from -9999 to 9999, when you pick up an item, it gets stored in your inv, if you have multiple of them, they stack. Kinda risk of rain vibe I guess

ChatGPT said:

Yeah, that’s doable — but raw -9999..9999 on everything will turn your game into either:

“everything instantly dies / nothing matters”
or
“one roll bricks the run permanently,”
unless you design the math so the chaos stays playable and funny, not just broken.

Here’s how to get the “super randomizer” vibe while keeping it a game.

1) Don’t randomize final stats uniformly

Uniform rand(-9999, 9999) is the fastest route to nonsense.

Instead, randomize a roll value, then transform it into stats with a distribution that produces:

lots of small/moderate rolls
occasional big spikes
extremely rare “god / cursed” extremes
Good chaos distributions (pick one)
Normal-ish (most sane): sum a few random numbers → bell curve
→ lots of mid rolls, rare extremes
Heavy-tail (Risk-of-Rain-ish insanity): Cauchy / Pareto / “exploding dice”
→ mostly normal, sometimes stupid
Tiered rarity: common / rare / legendary / cursed, each with its own range

If you want “extremes exist,” do heavy-tail but with guardrails (below).

2) Use “affixes” not “everything changes everything”

Make items give 1–3 effects, not 12 stats at once.

Example item:

“Glass Tooth”
+Damage (rolled)
-Max HP (rolled)

That keeps randomness legible and comedic: “I found a cracked ring that makes me a god but I sneeze and die.”

3) Stacking: don’t just add forever

If items stack infinitely and rolls can be ±9999, pure addition becomes unhinged too fast.

Use one of these stacking models:

A) Diminishing returns (best for sanity)
first copy is strong
later copies still matter but less

Example idea:

Effective bonus = roll * (1 + 0.6 + 0.36 + 0.216 + …) (a decay series)
B) Additive early, then “soft cap”
add normally until some threshold
beyond it, apply a softer slope
C) Multiplicative stacking for some stats only
Damage could stack multiplicatively (small numbers)
Flat HP could stack additively (bounded)
Cooldown reduction should be capped (always)
4) Negative rolls must create interesting problems, not dead runs

If an item can roll -9000 move speed, that’s not “risk,” that’s “uninstall.”

So give negatives counterplay:

negatives can be cleansed
negatives can be flipped by another item
negatives only apply under conditions (e.g., “while above 50% HP”)

Or: negative rolls turn into curses that are strong and dangerous:

“-3000 HP, but you revive once”
“-80% damage, but each kill permanently increases damage this run”

The player should think: “This is horrifying… but maybe it’s worth it.”

5) Make stats “bounded in effect” even if numbers look huge

You can still show crazy numbers, but the game uses functions that prevent hard breaks.

Examples:

Move speed: clamp to a minimum and maximum, or use square root scaling
Damage: allow big, but enemy HP scales too (and avoid overflow)
Attack speed / cooldown: cap it, always (or asymptote toward 0)

So you can keep the -9999..9999 aesthetic while the underlying effect stays within playable limits.

6) “Super Randomizer” needs a UI language

Players must understand what the hell happened.

Do:

show rolled value
show rarity tier
show what stacks
show set membership (if you keep sets too)

Also give players some control:

reroll once per level
scrap an item to remove its negative
convert 3 duplicates into 1 “stabilized” version

This keeps chaos fun instead of pure slot machine.

7) A really solid structure for your idea

Items stack (duplicates stack), but each pickup rolls ONE of:

Blessed (positive-heavy)
Normal (mixed)
Cursed (negative-heavy but with a special upside)

And the roll magnitude uses a heavy-tail distribution so you occasionally get:

“+4200 damage ring”
“-3000 HP amulet”
“+9999 luck but enemies spawn faster”

That’s the vibe you’re aiming for.

If you answer these two, I can propose a concrete “randomizer spec” (ranges, distributions, stacking rules) that will actually play well:

Do you want duplicates to add the roll (10 copies of +50 damage = +500), or do you want duplicates to reroll and then combine (like upgrading the item)?
